newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa sets racial quotas for national sports.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa sets racial quotas for national sports.

text.p: South African officials vowed on Monday to enforce a quota system to groom black athletes in the sports-mad country.

"Affirmative action is not a choice. It is a necessity. It is about transforming sport as an institution," the country's umbrella National Sports Council (NSC) said in a plan ratified by 60 sporting codes at the weekend.
The NSC said the policy was intended to bring blacks, women and the disabled into national teams.
South African teams which compete in the international arena -- apart from the national soccer squad -- mostly comprise whites, who benefited from better training and facilities under apartheid.

Despite three years of rule by President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress there has been little change in the country's sporting complexion and pressure has been growing on sports officials to give more money and attention to development projects.
The council said all sports codes were expected to set realistic targets in the short term, but gave no dates for meeting the quotas.

"Sports organisations' representative teams must at all times and at all levels have at least 40 percent representation with an escalating scale... There should be a bigger representation of black and women athletes in junior teams," the policy document said.
The plan is intended to advance blacks and other "previously disadvantaged" people fill places, but would not necessarily mean immediate selections for senior teams on the basis of race.
Junior teams could begin the process to ensure blacks and women reached levels where they would be selected for senior teams on merit. The quota would also apply to officials, staff and coaches.
The move prompted a bitter response from the former ruling National Party, which imposed segregation on the country's sports fields during four decades of apartheid rule.
"It is a pity that the NSC continually wants to remind South Africa of skin colour in this way -- at the expense of sport," said party spokesman Nic Koornhof.
"Affirmative action sometimes succeeds in team sports, but how will it succeed at individual level with the sportsmen and women making fools of themselves?," he asked.
The right-wing Conservative Party, which boycotted the all-race elections which swept Mandela into power in 1994, said the decision would not serve the interests of sport.
"(It) is one of the most racist decisions yet to be taken in the so-called new South Africa," said spokesman Pieter Aucamp.
The national rugby union spent around $4 million last year on development, while the cricket board budgeted over $1 million to promote the sport in black townships last summer.
Efforts such as these have had some effect at the lower levels, with township children forming teams and winning positions in provincial schools-level sides.
